haiku-low.q1: Split into pages of 500 products, ordered by product id ascending, fetched one at a time; never in parallel.
haiku-low.q2: In sync_state, as a cursor (last product id), written in the same transaction as each page's products, so it never runs ahead of saved data.
haiku-low.q3: Changes after start_seq are replayed from /catalogue/changes; a change applies only if its change_seq exceeds the staging row's, so newer copies are kept.
haiku-low.q4: Server returns 410 resync_required; client must download everything again, starting a full download from step 1.
haiku-low.q5: Built in products_staging by full download and catch-up, then swapped into products in one transaction; reps see the old catalogue until then.
haiku-low.q6: App launch or returning to foreground, at most once every 15 minutes since the last attempt; skipped during a full download.
haiku-low.q7: Retry same request after waiting 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, up to 5 attempts total; then stop, keep saved data, wait for next trigger.
haiku-low.q8: It finishes the current page, then pauses, and resumes from the saved cursor when Wi-Fi returns.
haiku-low.q9: Only if its change_seq is higher than the held row's; otherwise skipped.
haiku-low.q10: Starts from last_seq saved in sync_state; moves forward with each response's changes, saved in one transaction with the new last_seq.
haiku-low.q11: It reads Postgres product rows by change_seq; deletes are tombstone rows with deleted = true, kept 7 days.

sonnet.q1: Keyset pagination: pages of 500 products ordered by product id ascending, cursor = last product id received. Pages are fetched one at a time, never in parallel.
sonnet.q2: In the sync_state SQLite table (full-download cursor). Each page's products are written to products_staging and the cursor moved to the page's last product id in one transaction, so the cursor is never ahead of saved data.
sonnet.q3: POST /catalogue/full/start records start_seq (highest change_seq). After the last page, the client calls /catalogue/changes from start_seq until has_more is false, applying each change to staging (higher change_seq wins; deletes remove the row), before swapping.
sonnet.q4: The server returns HTTP 410 with body resync_required. The client must download everything again (full download restart); the old catalogue stays visible until the swap.
sonnet.q5: It is built in the products_staging table (cleared first, filled by pages, then caught up with changes). In one SQLite transaction at the swap, products is replaced with staging, last_seq set, staging cleared; the app reads the new catalogue only after that swap.
sonnet.q6: App launch or the app returning to foreground, at most once every 15 minutes measured from the last attempt (success or not, saved in sync_state). Skipped while a full download is in progress. Any network allowed.
sonnet.q7: Retry the same request, waiting 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, 16 s, at most 5 attempts in total. Then stop, keep saved data, and wait for the next trigger.
sonnet.q8: It finishes the page it is on, then pauses, and resumes from the cursor when Wi-Fi returns.
sonnet.q9: It applies the change only if its change_seq is higher than the change_seq on the existing row (or no row exists, for an update); otherwise it is skipped. A delete removes the row.
sonnet.q10: It asks /catalogue/changes?after_seq=<last_seq>. last_seq moves forward in the same transaction that writes each response's changes (one transaction per response), repeating while has_more is true.
sonnet.q11: It reads the change_seq on product rows in Postgres (rows with change_seq greater than n, in order). Deletes are tombstones: rows kept with deleted = true, purged after 7 days, and included in the changes feed.
